questions.question: A pulse travels along a stretched rope. What moves from one end of the rope to the other?
options: Energy and momentum carried by the disturbance
The rope material as a whole
Every rope particle at the pulse speed
A permanent displacement of all particles
questions.explanation: The disturbance transfers energy and momentum while rope particles oscillate locally. The medium does not undergo net transport with the travelling pattern.
questions.sourceEvidence: A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy and momentum without requiring a net transport of matter.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing propagation of a wave pattern with bulk transport of the medium

questions.question: Which wave can propagate through an empty vacuum?
options: A compression wave in a spring
questions.explanation: Electric and magnetic field oscillations can travel without a material medium. Sound, water waves, and spring compressions require matter whose particles respond.
questions.sourceEvidence: Electromagnetic waves are oscillations of electric and magnetic fields and can cross a vacuum.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming every wave requires a material medium

questions.question: How does a pulse differ from a periodic wave?
options: A pulse carries matter, while a periodic wave does not
A pulse is one disturbance, while a periodic wave repeats
A periodic wave can only exist in a vacuum
questions.explanation: A pulse occurs once while a periodic wave reproduces its pattern in time and space. The distinction is repetition rather than matter transport, speed, or medium type.
questions.sourceEvidence: A pulse is a single disturbance, whereas a periodic wave repeats in time and space.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Defining pulse versus periodic behaviour by medium or transport rather than repetition

questions.question: Which quantity is the maximum displacement of a medium particle from equilibrium?
questions.explanation: Amplitude measures the greatest displacement away from equilibrium. Wavelength is a spatial separation and frequency is a cycle rate.
questions.sourceEvidence: Amplitude measures the maximum displacement from equilibrium, wavelength is the distance between equal-phase points, and frequency counts cycles per second.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing amplitude with wavelength or frequency

questions.question: A periodic wave has a period of 0.25 seconds. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency is the reciprocal of period, so one divided by 0.25 seconds is 4 hertz. Multiplying by the period instead of taking its reciprocal gives the wrong cycle rate.
questions.sourceEvidence: The period is the time per cycle, so f = 1/T.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating period and frequency as directly proportional

questions.question: A source doubles its frequency while the wave remains in the same medium. What happens to wavelength?
options: It stays fixed while speed doubles
questions.explanation: The medium keeps the wave speed essentially fixed, so v = fλ requires wavelength to halve. Source frequency does not normally set a new speed in the unchanged medium.
questions.sourceEvidence: Wave speed is set mainly by the medium, not by the source frequency; changing frequency in one medium therefore changes wavelength.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming frequency changes wave speed instead of wavelength in one medium

questions.question: In which direction do particles oscillate in a longitudinal wave?
questions.explanation: Longitudinal oscillations lie parallel to the direction in which the wave travels. Perpendicular oscillation defines a transverse wave instead.
questions.sourceEvidence: For a transverse wave, oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of propagation; for a longitudinal wave, they are parallel.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Swapping transverse and longitudinal particle motion

questions.question: Which scientist formalised the secondary-wavelet construction used to explain diffraction?
questions.explanation: Christiaan Huygens described each wavefront point as a source of secondary wavelets. The other scientists are associated with relativity, induction, or quantum uncertainty.
questions.sourceEvidence: Christiaan Huygens formalised a wavefront construction in 1678, treating every point on a wavefront as a source of secondary wavelets.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Attributing Huygens wavefront construction to another physicist

questions.question: Two pulses overlap on a linear string. How is the instantaneous resultant displacement found?
questions.explanation: Linear superposition makes the resultant displacement the signed sum of the individual displacements. Multiplication, maximum selection, and speed averaging do not describe wave overlap.
questions.sourceEvidence: The superposition principle states that when waves overlap in a linear medium, the resultant displacement equals the algebraic sum of the individual displacements.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Adding wave magnitudes without respecting signed displacement

questions.question: What happens to two ideal pulses after they overlap and separate?
options: Each continues with its original form
questions.explanation: Ideal linear waves pass through overlap and then continue without permanent alteration. Temporary superposition does not make them merge, disappear, or swap frequencies.
questions.sourceEvidence: The waves do not permanently alter one another; after overlap, each continues with its original form in an ideal medium.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Believing interference permanently changes the component waves

questions.question: When do two equal waves produce maximum constructive interference?
options: A crest meets a trough half a cycle out of phase
A crest meets a crest in phase
questions.explanation: In-phase crests add to produce the largest resultant amplitude. A crest meeting a trough is the condition for cancellation rather than reinforcement.
questions.sourceEvidence: Constructive interference occurs where waves arrive in phase, so crest meets crest and their amplitudes add.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Reversing the phase conditions for constructive and destructive interference

questions.question: Two equal-amplitude waves arrive half a cycle out of phase. What is the result?
questions.explanation: Equal opposite displacements subtract to zero when the waves are half a cycle out of phase. Phase opposition changes resultant amplitude rather than doubling frequency automatically.
questions.sourceEvidence: Destructive interference occurs where waves arrive half a cycle out of phase, so crest meets trough and amplitudes subtract.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating half-cycle phase difference as reinforcement

questions.question: Which path difference produces destructive interference for equal coherent sources?
questions.explanation: A half-integer multiple of wavelength makes the arrivals opposite in phase. An integer multiple returns the waves to the same phase and produces constructive interference.
questions.sourceEvidence: For coherent sources with a constant phase difference, a path difference mλ produces constructive interference, while a path difference (m + 1/2)λ produces destructive interference.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Swapping the integer and half-integer path-difference conditions

questions.question: What forms when two equal-frequency waves travel in opposite directions?
questions.explanation: Oppositely travelling waves of the same frequency superpose into a standing-wave pattern. The result is neither charge flow nor a particle trajectory.
questions.sourceEvidence: Two equal-frequency waves travelling in opposite directions form a standing wave.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming oppositely travelling waves simply cancel everywhere

questions.question: Which statement correctly identifies nodes and antinodes in a standing wave?
options: Nodes have maximum amplitude and antinodes stay still
Both move with the wave speed
Nodes stay at zero displacement and antinodes have maximum amplitude
questions.explanation: Nodes are fixed cancellation points while antinodes undergo the largest oscillations. Reversing their roles misidentifies the defining features of the standing pattern.
questions.sourceEvidence: Nodes remain at zero displacement and antinodes oscillate with maximum amplitude.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Reversing the definitions of nodes and antinodes

questions.question: Why does a string fixed at both ends support discrete harmonics?
options: The string absorbs all nonzero amplitudes
Every frequency travels at a different speed
Only an integer number of half-wavelengths can fit its length
questions.explanation: Fixed boundaries require nodes at both ends, allowing only lengths containing integer half-wavelengths. The endpoints are nodes rather than antinodes, and the selection is a boundary condition.
questions.sourceEvidence: A string fixed at both ends supports only wavelengths that fit an integer number of half-wavelengths into its length, producing discrete harmonics.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Ignoring the fixed-end boundary condition when selecting standing-wave modes

questions.question: What is diffraction?
options: The spreading and bending of a wave at an edge or aperture
The permanent transfer of medium particles
The conversion of every wave into particles
The increase of wave speed with amplitude
questions.explanation: Diffraction describes how a wave spreads after encountering an opening or boundary edge. It is not bulk matter transport, a universal conversion, or an amplitude-speed rule.
questions.sourceEvidence: Diffraction is the spreading and bending of a wave as it passes an edge or aperture.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing diffraction with reflection or matter transport

questions.question: When is diffraction most pronounced?
options: When an opening is infinitely wider than the wavelength
When an opening is comparable to the wavelength
Only for waves in a vacuum
questions.explanation: An aperture comparable in size to the wavelength produces substantial spreading. A very large opening relative to wavelength gives much less noticeable diffraction.
questions.sourceEvidence: The effect is most pronounced when the opening or obstacle has a size comparable to the wavelength.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming diffraction is strongest through the widest opening

questions.question: How does Huygens' principle model a wavefront after an aperture?
options: Each exposed point launches a secondary wavelet
The aperture creates new matter particles
questions.explanation: Secondary wavelets from each exposed point combine to form the next wavefront. Restricting propagation to one ray cannot explain the observed spreading.
questions.sourceEvidence: Huygens’ principle explains the spreading by treating every exposed point on a wavefront as a source of secondary wavelets whose envelope forms the next wavefront.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Replacing Huygens wavelets with a single undeviated ray

questions.question: For a single slit of width a, what does a sin θ = mλ locate for nonzero integer m?
questions.explanation: The single-slit relation identifies angles where contributions across the slit cancel. It does not locate double-slit bright fringes or determine wave kinematics.
questions.sourceEvidence: Dark minima occur when a sin θ = mλ for nonzero integer m.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Using the single-slit minimum formula as a bright-fringe condition

questions.question: What happens to the central diffraction maximum when a single slit becomes narrower?
questions.explanation: A narrower slit requires a larger angle to reach the first cancellation minimum, widening the centre. Geometric intuition that a narrower opening must create a narrower wave pattern fails for diffraction.
questions.sourceEvidence: A narrower slit produces a wider central maximum because a larger angle is needed to establish the required path difference.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming a narrower slit creates a narrower diffraction pattern

questions.question: At fixed slit width, how does increasing wavelength affect the diffraction pattern?
questions.explanation: A larger wavelength requires larger minimum angles and therefore broadens the diffraction pattern. Wavelength changes angular structure rather than only the wave amplitude.
questions.sourceEvidence: Increasing wavelength has the same broadening effect.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Predicting that longer wavelength reduces diffraction

questions.question: Which change improves the diffraction-limited angular resolution of a telescope?
options: Use a longer wavelength at the same diameter
questions.explanation: Increasing aperture diameter reduces the Rayleigh angle and separates finer details. Longer wavelength or smaller diameter makes the diffraction limit worse.
questions.sourceEvidence: Larger telescope mirrors and shorter wavelengths therefore reveal finer structure.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing brightness with diffraction-limited resolution

questions.question: If both wavelength λ and aperture diameter D double, what happens to the Rayleigh angular limit 1.22λ/D?
questions.explanation: Doubling numerator and denominator leaves their ratio and the angular limit unchanged. Changing only one factor would alter resolution, but equal scaling cancels.
questions.sourceEvidence: The Rayleigh criterion gives an angular resolution of approximately 1.22λ/D for a circular aperture of diameter D.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Scaling wavelength or aperture without considering their ratio

questions.question: Whose double-slit experiment supplied decisive evidence for the wave behaviour of light?
questions.explanation: Thomas Young used two slits to produce the characteristic interference pattern of light waves. The other scientists are linked to induction or photoelectric measurements.
questions.sourceEvidence: Thomas Young’s double-slit experiment provided decisive evidence for the wave behaviour of light.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Attributing Young's double-slit result to another experimental physicist

questions.question: Why do the two narrow slits need a common monochromatic source?
options: To make each slit emit a different random frequency
To act as coherent secondary sources
questions.explanation: A common monochromatic source gives the slits a stable phase relationship needed for visible fringes. Random independent phases would average the interference away.
questions.sourceEvidence: A monochromatic source illuminates two narrow, closely spaced slits that act as coherent secondary sources.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming unrelated slit sources maintain a stable interference pattern

questions.question: What path difference produces a bright double-slit fringe?
questions.explanation: An integer number of wavelengths brings the two arrivals back into phase. A half-integer difference produces destructive rather than bright interference.
questions.sourceEvidence: Bright fringes occur where the path difference is an integer multiple of wavelength.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Using the destructive half-integer condition for a bright fringe

questions.question: For slit separation d, which relation gives the angle of a bright fringe?
options: d cos θ = λ/2 for all fringes
a sin θ = mλ with a as single-slit width
questions.explanation: The double-slit bright-fringe condition equates d sin θ to an integer wavelength multiple. The single-slit width formula locates diffraction minima instead.
questions.sourceEvidence: For slit separation d and screen distance L much larger than d, the angle to a bright fringe satisfies d sin θ = mλ.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Using single-slit width in place of double-slit separation

questions.question: If screen distance L doubles while λ and d remain fixed, what happens to adjacent-fringe spacing?
questions.explanation: The small-angle spacing λL/d is directly proportional to screen distance. An inverse dependence on L would contradict the geometry of a more distant screen.
questions.sourceEvidence: At small angles, sin θ is approximately y/L, so adjacent bright fringes are separated by Δy ≈ λL/d.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating fringe spacing as inversely proportional to screen distance

questions.question: How does increasing slit separation d affect the double-slit fringe pattern?
options: It spreads the fringes farther apart
questions.explanation: Fringe spacing is inversely proportional to slit separation, so larger d brings fringes closer. Greater separation does not remove the zero-order fringe or change wavelength.
questions.sourceEvidence: Larger wavelength or screen distance increases fringe spacing, while greater slit separation compresses the pattern.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Treating slit separation as directly proportional to fringe spacing

questions.question: What appears when photons are sent through a double slit one at a time for a long experiment?
options: A continuous smear from each individual photon
Localised impacts that build an interference distribution
No detections until two photons overlap
questions.explanation: Each event is localised, but many events accumulate according to an interference probability distribution. The pattern does not require photons to collide or arrive in pairs.
questions.sourceEvidence: When electrons, neutrons, atoms, or photons are sent through the apparatus one at a time, individual detections appear as localised impacts but gradually build an interference distribution.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Believing single-particle interference requires particles to collide with each other

questions.question: What happens when reliable which-path information is obtained in a double-slit experiment?
options: Every particle stops at the slit
questions.explanation: Path information makes the alternatives distinguishable, preventing their amplitudes from producing the same interference terms. The effect concerns measurement context rather than particle speed or automatic geometric rescaling.
questions.sourceEvidence: Obtaining reliable which-path information removes the interference because the alternatives become distinguishable.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming path information can be acquired without affecting interference

questions.question: As a mechanical wave travels through a medium, what do the medium particles normally do?
options: Travel with the wave across the entire medium
Move only in the propagation direction
questions.explanation: Medium particles oscillate around their local equilibrium positions while the pattern propagates. Following the wave across the medium would imply net matter transport that is not normally present.
questions.sourceEvidence: Particles of a mechanical medium oscillate around equilibrium; they do not normally travel with the wave.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Confusing local particle oscillation with wave propagation

questions.question: A wave crosses into a new medium. Which quantity remains fixed by the source?
questions.explanation: The source continues to set the oscillation frequency across the boundary. The new medium may change speed and wavelength together.
questions.sourceEvidence: Frequency is fixed by the source and remains unchanged at a boundary, while speed and wavelength may change.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Changing frequency at a boundary instead of speed and wavelength

questions.question: In a linear medium, what does increasing wave amplitude not automatically increase?
questions.explanation: Linear wave speed is controlled mainly by medium properties rather than amplitude. Amplitude directly describes displacement and commonly affects transported energy.
questions.sourceEvidence: Amplitude is not wavelength, and increasing amplitude does not automatically increase wave speed in a linear medium.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Equating larger amplitude with greater wave speed

questions.question: Which path difference gives complete destructive interference for equal amplitudes?
questions.explanation: A half-integer wavelength difference makes equal waves arrive in opposite phase and cancel. An integer wavelength difference produces constructive alignment.
questions.sourceEvidence: Constructive interference occurs at Δr = mλ, while complete destructive interference for equal amplitudes occurs at Δr = (m + 1/2)λ.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Swapping constructive and destructive path-difference formulas

questions.question: Which formula-feature pairing is correct?
options: a sin θ = mλ locates single-slit dark minima
a sin θ = mλ locates double-slit bright maxima
d sin θ = mλ locates single-slit dark minima
d sin θ = mλ gives wave speed
questions.explanation: The aperture width a belongs to the single-slit cancellation condition for dark minima. Double-slit bright maxima use slit separation d instead.
questions.sourceEvidence: In single-slit diffraction, a sin θ = mλ identifies dark minima; in a double slit, d sin θ = mλ identifies bright maxima.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Interchanging slit width and slit separation formulas

questions.question: When is the approximation y ≈ L sin θ appropriate?
options: For every angle including ninety degrees
For small θ with a distant screen
Only when L equals the slit separation
questions.explanation: The screen-coordinate approximation follows from small-angle geometry and a screen distant relative to the slits. Using it at large angles treats an approximation as an identity.
questions.sourceEvidence: The relation y ≈ L sin θ is accurate only when θ is small and the screen is distant relative to the slit separation.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Using a small-angle approximation outside its geometric range

questions.question: Which order labels the central double-slit fringe?
questions.explanation: Zero path difference at the centre corresponds to order m = 0. Beginning the count at one omits the central maximum.
questions.sourceEvidence: Keep units consistent, convert nanometres before substitution, and include the central fringe as m = 0.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Omitting the zero-order central fringe or failing to convert wavelength units

questions.question: Why do two unrelated light sources usually fail to produce a stable interference pattern?
options: Their phase difference varies too rapidly
questions.explanation: Rapidly changing relative phase makes bright and dark contributions average to nearly uniform intensity. Interference requires coherence rather than zero momentum or an inability to diffract.
questions.sourceEvidence: Finally, an interference pattern requires coherence; unrelated sources with rapidly varying phase differences average to uniform intensity.
questions.misconceptionTargeted: Assuming any two overlapping sources produce stable fringes without coherence
